abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) driven by reward prediction errors (RPEs) enables adaptive behavior across species. While midbrain-striatal encoding of RPEs is well-documented, how prefrontal circuits translate these signals into species-specific flexibility remains unknown. Integrating cross-species RL modeling, neuroimaging, and transcriptomics, we identified shared molecular and neuroanatomical infrastructure for RPE computation in humans and macaques. Despite this conserved foundation, humans demonstrated superior performance on deterministic and probabilistic reversal tasks. Single-trial decoding revealed equally robust dynamic RPE-to-choice prediction in both species; yet humans disproportionately recruited dorsal anterior cingulate (dACC) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC). Interspecies alignment localized similarly predictive policy signals in macaque dACC/dlPFC that failed to guide behavior. Crucially, a within-species comparison in an independent human cohort demonstrated that only near-optimal performers exhibited strong prefrontal action decoding, contrasting with suboptimal individuals. These findings suggest that behavioral flexibility arises from prefrontal readout breadth - a hierarchical scaling principle that challenges efficient coding theories.
